claim: Two macaque monkeys grasped a large set of 49 objects causing highly variable visual stimuli and motor responses.
source: Two macaque monkeys grasped a large set of 49 objects causing highly variable visual stimuli and motor responses (Figure 1a–b, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this experimental design in the Results section, supported by reference to figures and video.

claim: Hand and arm kinematics were recorded from an instrumented glove in 27 degrees of freedom.
source: During the experiments we recorded hand and arm kinematics from an instrumented glove (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2012) (see Figure 1c, Video 2) in conjunction with neuronal activity from 6 cortical microelectrode arrays (6 x 32 channels) (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: The manuscript describes the recording method with citation and references to figures showing the glove and recording setup.

claim: Neuronal activity was recorded from 6 cortical microelectrode arrays with 192 total channels.
source: During the experiments we recorded hand and arm kinematics from an instrumented glove (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2012) (see Figure 1c, Video 2) in conjunction with neuronal activity from 6 cortical microelectrode arrays (6 x 32 channels) (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of arrays and channels used for recording.

claim: Data was collected from 20 recording sessions across two macaque monkeys (10 sessions per animal).
source: We analysed data from 20 recording sessions of two macaque monkeys (10 sessions per animal).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of recording sessions analyzed.

claim: On average, 202 ± 7 and 355 ± 20 single and multiunits were collected per session in monkey Z and M, respectively.
source: On average, spiking activity of 202 ± 7 and 355 ± 20 (mean ± s.d.) single and multiunits were collected in each session in monkey Z and M, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on the number of units recorded.

claim: 29.2% and 25.2% of recorded units were from AIP in monkey Z and M, respectively.
source: Of these units, 29.2% and 25.2% were recorded from AIP, 37.3% and 32.3% from F5, and 33.5% and 42.5% from M1 (monkey Z and M, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of units recorded from each brain area.

claim: Presenting 3D objects to the monkeys led to vigorous discharge of AIP neurons.
source: Presenting 3D objects to the monkeys lead to vigorous discharge (Baumann et al., 2009; Murata et al., 2000) of AIP-neurons (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with supporting citations and references to figures showing neural responses.

claim: The modulated AIP population was significantly larger and faster appearing after stimulus onset than in F5.
source: The modulated population was not only larger (sliding ANOVA, Figure 3), but also significantly faster appearing after stimulus onset than in F5 (49.7 ms and 54.9 ms, monkey M and Z respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing measurements and statistical analysis comparing AIP and F5 responses.

claim: Individual AIP cells were capable of differentiating object shapes at high precision.
source: Impressively, individual AIP cells were capable of differentiating object shapes at high precision (e.g., Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with reference to example data in a figure.

claim: An example AIP neuron could significantly separate 71% of the 946 condition pairs during the cue epoch.
source: Statistical analysis between all conditions (ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey-Kramer criterion, p<0.01; see Materials and methods) revealed a high encoding capacity of the example neuron that could significantly separate 71% of the 946 condition pairs (44 conditions).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results for an example neuron's discriminative capacity.

claim: The example AIP neuron decreased its modulation depth in darkness but maintained its encoding of shape.
source: Interestingly, the neuron decreased its MD in darkness but maintained its encoding of shape (as also indicated in Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript describes this observation with reference to figure data.

claim: Objects were separated in the AIP population based on their shape, independent of how they were grasped.
source: In this N-space of AIP, we found objects to be separated based on their shape. Independent of the way the objects were grasped, the neural space accurately differentiated horizontal cylinders (black), vertical cylinders (green), rings (magenta), spheres (orange), cubes (blue), and bars (black) (see Video 3 for an animated 3D view of a typical N-space).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering pattern observed in the neural space with reference to figures and video.

claim: 100% and 91% of objects shared their cluster with other objects of the same shape during the cue and grasp epoch, respectively, in AIP.
source: 100% and 91% of the objects shared their cluster with other objects of the same shape during the cue and grasp epoch, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative results from hierarchical cluster analysis.

claim: The AIP population encoded the size of objects, but differentiated this geometrical feature at clearly lower neural modulations compared to object shape.
source: The AIP population also encoded the size of objects, but differentiated this geometrical feature at clearly lower neural modulations compared to object shape.
evidence: The manuscript describes a comparison of neural modulations for different object features.

claim: The AIP population responded highly similarly to the presentation of mixed and abstract objects during the cue epoch.
source: Strikingly, the AIP population responded highly similar to the presentation (cue epoch) of mixed (Figure 3b) and abstract (Figure 3e) objects (t-test, p>0.05; 35% vs. 35% and 20% vs. 17% comparing mixed and abstract objects in monkey Z and M, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of population responses to different object sets.

claim: The equal responses of AIP to both mixed and abstract object sets strongly supports the specialisation of AIP in processing object shapes.
source: Thus, the equal responses to both object sets strongly supports the specialisation of AIP in processing object shapes.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the comparison of responses to different object sets.

claim: AIP remained the most tuned area when the monkeys planned and grasped the abstract objects.
source: Importantly, AIP remained the most tuned area when the monkeys planned and grasped the abstract objects, as shown in Figure 3e.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to figure data.

claim: The number of significantly tuned AIP cells decreased during planning and grasping epochs for abstract objects compared to mixed objects.
source: However, the number of significantly tuned cells decreased during these epochs in comparison to the responses evoked by the mixed objects (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript describes a comparison of tuning across different object sets and task epochs.

claim: Precision and power grips on the same handle were located most distantly in the kinematic space but closest to each other in the N-space of AIP.
source: Although both conditions were located most distantly in the kinematic or joint-angle (J-) space in both monkeys (see Figure 4e and 5a), they were located closest to each other in the N-space of AIP (see Figure 2e–f), clearly implying a visual representation of the handle.
evidence: The manuscript compares the representation of the same object grasped differently in kinematic and neural spaces.

claim: 21% and 16% of AIP neurons were significantly tuned to differentiate precision and power grips on the handle in monkey Z and M, respectively.
source: Statistical analysis revealed, however, that both conditions (00, 01) slightly increased their neural distance (Figure 2d) towards planning and movement execution, as expressed by an average of 21% and 16% of significantly tuned AIP neurons in monkey Z and M (ANOVA tested in grasp epoch, p<0.01).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from statistical analysis of neural tuning.

claim: AIP widely maintained its coding for visual object properties during movement execution in the dark, although with significantly smaller neural distances.
source: AIP also widely maintained its coding for visual object properties during movement execution in the dark (Figure 2f), although with significantly smaller neural distances (Figure 2e–f).
evidence: The manuscript describes the persistence of visual coding across task epochs with reference to figures.

claim: AIP serves as working memory and not only extracts, but also maintains visual object information required for motor planning and execution.
source: We hypothesize that AIP serves as working memory and not only extracts, but also maintains visual object information required for motor planning and execution (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a hypothesis based on the observed data, with supporting citation.

claim: The F5 population was strongly activated in the motor epochs when the mixed objects were grasped differently.
source: The F5 population was strongly activated in the motor epochs when the mixed objects were grasped differently (up to 47% and 45% tuned neurons in monkey Z and M resp., see Figure 3b), and it was strikingly unmodulated when the abstract objects were grasped similar (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of tuned neurons with reference to figures.

claim: The F5 population was strikingly unmodulated when the abstract objects were grasped similarly.
source: The F5 population was strongly activated in the motor epochs when the mixed objects were grasped differently (up to 47% and 45% tuned neurons in monkey Z and M resp., see Figure 3b), and it was strikingly unmodulated when the abstract objects were grasped similar (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the lack of modulation for similar grips with reference to figures.

claim: The M1 population responded uniformly for similar grips but was modulated very strongly when different hand configurations were applied.
source: Likewise, the M1 population responded uniformly for similar grips (Figure 3e), but it was modulated very strongly when different hand configurations were applied (up to 67% and 61% in monkey Z an M resp, see Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript describes M1 population responses to different grip types with specific percentages.

claim: M1 showed no or minimal preparation activity during movement planning.
source: During movement planning, M1 showed no or minimal preparation activity (Figure 3a–c), whereas F5 revealed a multimodal role: in the cue epoch, the tuned F5 population substantially decreased from 28% to 18% in monkey Z, and from 13% to 4% in monkey M, when comparing abstract with mixed objects.
evidence: The manuscript describes the lack of planning activity in M1 with reference to figures.

claim: The tuned F5 population substantially decreased from 28% to 18% in monkey Z when comparing abstract with mixed objects during the cue epoch.
source: During movement planning, M1 showed no or minimal preparation activity (Figure 3a–c), whereas F5 revealed a multimodal role: in the cue epoch, the tuned F5 population substantially decreased from 28% to 18% in monkey Z, and from 13% to 4% in monkey M, when comparing abstract with mixed objects.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages comparing F5 responses to different object sets.

claim: 18% and 4% of all F5 neurons in monkey Z and M respectively remained modulated when the monkeys observed the abstract geometries.
source: However, 18% and 4% (Monkey Z and M resp.) of all F5 neurons remained their modulation when the monkeys observed the abstract geometries. Thus, at least some F5 cells coded objects in purely visual terms.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and draws a conclusion about visual coding in F5.

claim: 76% of the visual and 72% of visuomotor tuned neurons recorded from F5 were detected on the ventral site.
source: In fact, 76% of the visual (abstract objects) and 72% of visuomotor tuned neurons (mixed objects) recorded from F5 were detected on the ventral site (ANOVA p<0.01, all sessions, tested in cue epoch), in line with previously reported enhanced decoding capabilities of planning signals from ventral F5 (Schaffelhofer et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from statistical analysis with supporting citation.

claim: The dorsal F5 array mainly contributed during movement execution by a four-fold increase of its tuned population with respect to the cue epoch.
source: In contrast, the dorsal F5 array, corresponding to F5p, mainly contributed during movement execution by a four-fold increase of its tuned population with respect to the cue epoch.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of neural tuning in dorsal F5.

claim: An example F5 neuron demonstrated a maximum modulation depth of 39.8 Hz while grasping and allowed significantly separating 42% of all condition pairs.
source: The example neuron shown in Figure 4a–b demonstrated a maximum MD of 39.8 Hz while grasping and allowed significantly separating 42% of all condition pairs in this epoch (Figure 4b, right).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measures for an example neuron with reference to figures.

claim: The example F5 neuron showed similar motor coding during the preparation epoch (r = 0.76 correlation between plan and grasp MD-maps).
source: Importantly, the neuron showed similar motor coding already during the preparation epoch (r = 0.76, between plan and grasp MD-maps, as shown in Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific correlation coefficient with reference to figures.

claim: Using the planning activity of the example F5 neuron alone, about 43% of the task conditions could be separated.
source: Using the planning activity of the example neuron alone, about 43% of the task conditions could be separated, thereby demonstrating the important role of F5 for hand movement planning.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage and draws a conclusion about F5's role in planning.

claim: The J-space closely reflected the hand's wrist orientation (1st principal component) and hand aperture (2nd principal component).
source: The J-space demonstrated a high variability of hand configurations across conditions and closely reflected the hand's wrist orientation (1st principal component) and hand aperture (2nd principal component).
evidence: The manuscript describes the interpretation of principal components in the kinematic space.

claim: Objects of small sizes were grasped similarly and were located close to each other in the reduced and complete J-space.
source: (1) Objects of small sizes such as the small rings (condition ID 21, 22), spheres (11,41,42) and cubes (31, 32) were grasped similarly (index finger and thumb) and thus were located close to each other in the reduced and the complete J-space.
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering of objects in kinematic space based on grip similarity.

claim: Vertical cylinders and big rings were enclosed with the digits and required 90° of wrist rotation, locating them close to each other in J-space.
source: (2) Vertical cylinders and big rings (16, 23–26, 71–76) were enclosed with the digits and required 90° of wrist rotation. Therefore, these grips are located close to each other in J-space.
evidence: The manuscript describes the kinematic similarity and spatial clustering of specific grip types.

claim: All abstract objects shared a compact cluster in J-space, demonstrating their similarity.
source: (3) All abstract objects (91–96) shared a compact cluster and demonstrated their similarity in J-space.
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering pattern of abstract objects in kinematic space.

claim: Precision and power grips performed on the same handle required highly different hand configurations and were located distant in J-space.
source: (4) Precision (00) and power grips (01) performed on the same handle required highly different hand configurations and were located distant in J-space.
evidence: The manuscript describes the kinematic dissimilarity of different grip types on the same object.

claim: The majority of kinematic observations were also found in the N-space of F5 during motor execution.
source: Importantly, the majority of kinematic observations were also found in the N-space of F5 during motor execution (Figure 4h).
evidence: The manuscript describes the similarity between kinematic and neural representations with reference to figures.

claim: Conditions of different visual stimuli but equal grips were located close to each other in the F5 neural space during motor execution.
source: In contrast to AIP, conditions of different visual stimuli but equal grips were located close to each other in the neural space (observation 1–3), whereas conditions of similar visual stimuli but different motor responses caused a separation (observation 4–5).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering pattern in F5 neural space based on motor rather than visual features.

claim: The findings demonstrate clearly different coding properties between AIP and F5 and reveal a primary motor role of F5 during movement execution.
source: These results were further supported by the high similarity between the J- (Figure 4e) and N-space (Figure 4h) during movement execution (for quantification see section 'Numerical comparison' and Figure 7). The findings demonstrate clearly different coding properties with respect to AIP and reveal a primary motor role of F5 during movement execution.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the comparison of neural representations across areas.

claim: The F5 population demonstrated first modulations and expressions of the upcoming motor actions already during motor preparation.
source: Similar to observations at the single unit level (see Figure 4a–b), the F5 population demonstrated first modulations and expressions of the upcoming motor actions already during motor preparation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of F5 population activity with reference to figures.

claim: Abstract forms, small objects, as well as the big rings and cylinders created individual clusters in the J-space and were located close to each other.
source: In accordance with the low-dimensional representation, abstract forms, small objects, as well as the big rings and cylinders created individual clusters in the J-space and were located close to each other.
evidence: The manuscript describes the hierarchical clustering results in kinematic space.

claim: Motor characteristics were rudimentarily marked in F5 already during motor preparation and persisted to a large extent during motor execution.
source: As shown in Figure 5b, these motor characteristics were rudimentarily marked in F5 already during motor preparation (see Figure 5b, coloured boxes). These clusters that emerged during motor planning persisted to a large extent during motor execution, but increased their relative distance to each other (Figure 5c), in line with the higher MD of single F5 neurons during grasp execution (Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal evolution of motor representations in F5 with reference to figures.

claim: Premotor preparation activity primarily originated from the ventral F5 array.
source: As discussed above, premotor preparation activity primarily originated from the ventral F5 array. Thus, the modulations observed prior to movement execution, such as observed in the CDA and hierarchical clustering, are mainly based on the ventral recording site.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical source of preparation signals based on earlier analysis.

claim: Both F5 arrays significantly supported movement execution.
source: In contrast, both arrays significantly supported movement execution.
evidence: The manuscript describes the contribution of both recording sites to motor execution.

claim: The different modalities in both F5 recording sites are in line with the architectonically and connectionally distinct subdivisions F5a and F5p.
source: The different modalities in both recording sites are in line with the architectonically (Belmalih et al., 2009) and connectionally (Borra et al., 2010; Gerbella et al., 2011) distinct subdivisions F5a and F5p, which largely correspond to the ventral and dorsal recording array, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript relates the observed functional differences to known anatomical subdivisions with supporting citations.

claim: Distinct connections of F5a with SII, AIP and other subdivision of F5 (but not to M1) suggest an integration of visual, motor and context specific information.
source: Distinct connections of F5a with SII, AIP and other subdivision of F5 (but not to M1) (Gerbella et al., 2011) suggest an integration of visual, motor and context specific information (Theys et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from known anatomical connections with supporting citations.

claim: Connections of F5p to the hand area of M1 and to the spinal cord suggest a rather direct contribution to hand movement control.
source: On the other hand, connections of F5p to the hand area of M1 and to the spinal cord (Borra et al., 2010) suggest a rather direct contribution to hand movement control.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from known anatomical connections with supporting citation.

claim: The multimodal preparation signals and distinct motor feature coding support the key role of F5 for visuomotor transformation.
source: Taken together, the multimodal preparation signals, including visual and motor contribution, and the distinct motor feature coding towards planning and execution, supports the key role of F5 for visuomotor transformation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the observed data patterns.

claim: Single neurons of M1 were almost exclusively modulated during movement execution and showed minimal modulations during preparatory epochs.
source: In agreement with the general population response (Figure 3b), single neurons of M1 were almost exclusively modulated during movement execution and showed minimal modulations during preparatory epochs (Umilta et al., 2007), as also indicated by the example neuron in Figure 6a–b.
evidence: The manuscript describes M1 neuron properties with supporting citation and reference to figures.

claim: An example M1 neuron was capable of differentiating 52% of condition pairs when holding the object, but failed to separate any (0%) of the conditions when planning the movement.
source: This neuron was capable of differentiating 52% of condition pairs when holding the object, but failed to separate any (0%) of the conditions when planning the movement. (ANOVA, Tukey-Kramer criterion, p<0.01), thereby highlighting its major difference to F5 neurons.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages from statistical analysis of an example neuron.

claim: PCRA analysis revealed striking similarities between the J-space and the N-space of M1.
source: Similar to the analysis performed on the F5 population, PCRA analysis compared the J-space with the N-space of M1 and revealed, highly important for the understanding of hand movement generation and as an important control, striking similarities between both representations, as demonstrated in Figure 6c,e.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of PCRA analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The large majority of conditions were assigned to the same clusters in the J- and the M1-space.
source: The large majority of conditions were assigned to the same clusters in the J- and the M1-space (coloured boxes in Figure 6d,f, exceptions: conditions 42, 43).
evidence: The manuscript describes the hierarchical clustering results with reference to figures.

claim: All of the motor characteristics defined were observed and were even more strongly represented in M1 than in F5.
source: Furthermore, all of the motor characteristics (1–5) defined above were also observed and were even more strongly represented in M1 than in F5: again, the group of small objects (11, 21–22, 31–32, 41–42) and the group of abstract forms (91–96) created strong and individual clusters, whereas small (21–22) and big rings (16, 23–26) as well as precision (00) and power grips (01) were located distant from each other.
evidence: The manuscript describes the comparison of motor representations between M1 and F5.

claim: M1 demonstrated the highest similarity to the J-space (averaged value across 10 recording sessions for monkey M: 0.48, for monkey Z: 0.59).
source: In accordance with the previous analysis, M1 demonstrated the highest similarity to the J-space (averaged value across 10 recording sessions for monkey M: 0.48, for monkey Z: 0.59), followed by F5 (monkey M: 0.61; monkey Z: 0.65) and AIP (monkey M: 0.75; monkey Z: 0.75).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative similarity measures across recording sessions.

claim: Differences in motor similarity between areas AIP, F5, and M1 were significant.
source: Furthermore, differences between areas were significant (ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey-Kramer criterion, p<0.01).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results comparing areas.

claim: During object presentation, similar chequered patterns were found in area AIP in both animals on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: During object presentation, we found similar chequered patterns in area AIP in both animals (t1 in Figure 8), again confirming the coding of object shapes at the population level, but here on trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the feature correlation analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: Visual feature patterns caused a significant correlation peak between AIP and F5 in animal Z, suggesting the propagation of visual information.
source: These visual feature patterns caused a significant correlation peak with area F5 in animal Z, suggesting the propagation of visual information; in animal M, however, only a minor correlation peak was observed (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation analysis results with reference to figures and draws an inference about information flow.

claim: F5 and AIP demonstrated minimal similarities during movement planning.
source: Interestingly, F5 and AIP demonstrated minimal similarities during movement planning, in support of the different encoding schemes of visual and motor features described at the population level (Figures 2,4 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: F5 modulations strongly increased before movement execution and were followed by M1 activity after movement onset.
source: F5 modulations strongly increased before movement execution and were followed by M1 activity after movement onset (see Video 5), suggesting that premotor cortex drives M1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of neural activity with reference to video and draws an inference about causal relationships.

claim: F5 and M1 signals followed in time and in modulation patterns, as expressed by impressively high correlation coefficients in both animals.
source: Signals did not only follow in time but also in modulation patterns, as expressed by the impressively high correlation coefficients in both animals (t2 in Figure 8), and in agreement with similar motor coding schemes observed with the population analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: Area AIP revealed a strong visual role and a specialisation for processing object shapes.
source: We show that the cortical grasping network differentiates visual from motor processes to achieve this transformation. Area AIP revealed a strong visual role and a specialisation for processing object shapes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: Area F5 coded objects only partially and temporarily in visual terms and switched to dominant motor signals towards movement planning and execution.
source: In contrast, area F5 coded objects only partially and temporarily in visual terms and switched to dominant motor signals towards movement planning and execution.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The encoded motor features of F5 showed striking similarities with M1, suggesting a strong collaboration of both areas during hand and movement control.
source: The encoded motor features of F5 showed striking similarities with M1 thereby suggesting a strong collaboration of both areas during hand and movement control.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this key finding in the Discussion section.

claim: AIP receives input from parietal visual areas (e.g., LIP, CIP, and V6a) as well as from the inferior temporal cortex (e.g., areas TEa and TEm).
source: AIP, an end-stage area of the dorsal visual stream, receives input from parietal visual areas (e.g., LIP, CIP, and V6a) as well as from the inferior temporal cortex (e.g., areas TEa and TEm) (Borra et al., 2008; Nakamura et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript describes known anatomical connections with supporting citations.

claim: AIP connects to premotor F5 via dense reciprocal projections.
source: AIP further connects to pre-motor F5 via dense reciprocal projections (Borra et al., 2008; Gerbella et al., 2011; Luppino et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript describes known anatomical connections with supporting citations.

claim: F5 has a significant connection with the hand area of M1.
source: Another significant connection links F5 with the hand area of M1 (Dum and Strick, 2005; Kraskov et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes known anatomical connections with supporting citations.

claim: Neurons of M1, in particular in the bank of the central sulcus, form direct connections to α-motor neurons in the spinal cord that drive the distal hand muscles.
source: As described by Rathelot and Strick (2009), neurons of M1, in particular in the bank of the central sulcus, form direct connections to α-motor neurons in the spinal cord that drive the distal hand muscles.
evidence: The manuscript describes known anatomical connections with supporting citation.

claim: The majority of M1-neurons demonstrated significant modulations during hand movement control despite highly constant reaching components.
source: In line with these observations, the majority of M1-neurons demonstrated significant modulations during hand movement control despite highly constant reaching components (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observed neural responses with reference to figures.

claim: Strong grasp modulations and their intercommunication confirmed the correct positioning of the electrode arrays and the importance of all areas for visuomotor processing.
source: Together, strong grasp modulations (Figure 3) and their intercommunication (Figure 8) confirmed the correct positioning of the electrode arrays and the importance of all areas for visuomotor processing.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the observed data patterns.

claim: The predominant criterion for object separation in AIP was object shape, even for abstract geometries that required the same grip.
source: The predominant criterion for object separation was object shape, even for abstract geometries that required the same grip (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding with reference to figures.

claim: AIP's shape coding findings are in agreement with anatomical connections to the inferior temporal cortex that codes perceived shapes.
source: These findings are in agreement with anatomical connections of AIP to the inferior temporal cortex (Borra et al., 2008) that codes perceived shapes (Logothetis et al., 1995; Tanaka, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript relates the findings to known anatomical and functional properties with supporting citations.

claim: Visual coding at the population level in AIP does not preclude motor coding of some individual cells.
source: We emphasize that visual coding at the population level does not preclude motor coding of some individual cells, as suggested previously (Murata et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the interpretation of population-level findings with supporting citation.

claim: The evidence of bidirectional connections to F5 suggests that subpopulations exist in AIP that reflect feedback of motor signals.
source: Rather, the evidence of bidirectional connections to F5 suggests that subpopulations exist in AIP that reflect feedback of motor signals.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from known anatomical connections.

claim: When grasping an object, both visual selection of object parts and selection of a corresponding hand configuration are required.
source: In fact, when grasping an object, both processes are required: the visual selection of (focus on) object parts and the selection of a corresponding hand configuration.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational requirements for grasping.

claim: The separation of the same object when grasped differently originated from one object shape cluster in AIP.
source: Second, the separation of the same object when grasped differently, originated from one object shape cluster.
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering pattern observed in AIP neural space.

claim: Baumann et al. (2009) demonstrated that AIP planning activity depends on the previous visual knowledge of an object.
source: In line with these findings, Baumann et al. (2009) demonstrated that AIP planning activity depends on the previous visual knowledge of an object (see Figure 6 in their paper).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to support the interpretation of the current findings.

claim: Presenting an object caused a strong visual activation in the AIP population that got separated when a grip type was instructed subsequently.
source: Presenting an object (the same handle as we used) caused a strong visual activation in the AIP population that got separated when a grip type (precision or power grip) was instructed subsequently.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from a cited study.

claim: Instructing the grip type before object presentation did not lead to a substantial population response in AIP and caused significant modulations only after the object was presented.
source: In contrast, instructing the grip type before object presentation did not lead to a substantial population response and caused significant modulations only after the object was presented.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from a cited study.

claim: The differentiation schemes in AIP support the hypothesis of visual rather than motor transformations.
source: These differentiation schemes support our hypothesis of visual rather than motor transformations in AIP.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the cited evidence.

claim: F5 is densely connected to AIP and has been associated with visuomotor processes.
source: F5 is densely connected to AIP (Borra et al., 2008; Gerbella et al., 2011; Luppino et al., 1999) and has been associated with these visuomotor processes (Fluet et al., 2010; Jeannerod et al., 1995; Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript describes known anatomical and functional properties with supporting citations.

claim: Neurons in F5 respond to the presentation of 3D objects.
source: Similar to AIP, neurons in F5 respond to the presentation of 3D objects (Fluet et al., 2010; Murata et al., 1997; Raos et al., 2006; Theys et al., 2012a; Vargas-Irwin et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes known functional properties with supporting citations.

claim: The study demonstrated for the first time that the F5 population does not reflect stereotypical grip types but represents a continuum of many hand configurations.
source: Due to the large number of objects tested, we could demonstrate for the first time that the F5 population does not reflect stereotypical grip types (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001), but represents a continuum of many hand configurations (Figure 5), highly similar to M1 (Figure 8, Video 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a novel finding with reference to figures and video.

claim: Motor characteristics in the N-Space of F5 could be observed not only in motor execution epochs, but also during motor preparation.
source: Importantly, motor characteristics in the N-Space of F5 could be observed not only in motor execution epochs, but also during motor preparation (Figure 4i, 5b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal dynamics of motor representations with reference to figures.

claim: F5 also contained a small subgroup of neurons that represented pure visual information during the cue epoch.
source: However, F5 also contained a small subgroup of neurons that represented pure visual information during the cue epoch (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the presence of visual neurons in F5 with reference to figures.

claim: The vast majority of visual F5 cells have been recorded from the ventral array, originating from the F5a subdivision.
source: The vast majority of these cells have been recorded from the ventral array, i.e., they originate from the F5a subdivision.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical location of visual neurons in F5.

claim: Visual F5 neurons might be crucially involved in the activation of stored motor plans.
source: We suggest that these neurons receive direct visual input from AIP and might be crucially involved in the activation of stored motor plans.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: Similar modulation patterns in AIP and F5 during object presentation suggest the communication of visual properties to premotor cortex.
source: Similar modulation patterns in AIP and F5 during object presentation suggest the communication of visual properties to premotor cortex (Figure 8 and Video 5).
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from the correlation analysis with reference to figures and video.

claim: The presence of multimodal signals and the proximity of specialized sub areas for visual input and motor output suggest a central role of F5 for visuomotor transformation.
source: The presence of multimodal signals as well as the proximity of specialized sub areas for visual input and motor output suggest a central role of F5 for visuomotor transformation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the observed data patterns.

claim: The hand area of primary motor cortex (M1) showed an almost exclusive role for motor execution.
source: In contrast to F5, the hand area of primary motor cortex (M1) showed an almost exclusive role for motor execution (Saleh et al., 2010; Umilta et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes M1's functional role with supporting citations.

claim: The study investigated, for the first time, the N-space of the hand area of M1 for a large repertoire of grasping actions.
source: We investigated, for the first time, the N-space of the hand area of M1 (Rathelot and Strick, 2009) for a large repertoire of grasping actions.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a novel contribution with supporting citation.

claim: The N-space of M1 was closely related to the J-space.
source: As expected, the N-space of M1 was closely related to the J-space (Figure 6) and showed the highest motor similarity across all three areas (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between neural and kinematic spaces with reference to figures.

claim: Correlating M1 modulation patterns with F5 revealed that both areas heavily share motor features for grasping.
source: Correlating these M1 modulation patterns with F5 revealed that both areas are not only strongly interconnected (Dum and Strick, 2005; Kraskov et al., 2011), but they also heavily share motor features for grasping (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation analysis results with supporting citations and reference to figures.

claim: The high similarity of the F5 and M1 population during movement execution is in agreement with findings of similar coding schemes between both areas in spiking and beta-band LFP activity.
source: The high similarity of the F5 and M1 population during movement execution (Figure 4h vs. Figure 6e, Figure 8, and Video 5) is in agreement with findings of similar coding schemes between both areas in spiking (Umilta et al., 2007) and beta-band LFP activity (Spinks et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript relates the findings to previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: The earlier premotor (vs. motor) onset suggests that the movement is facilitated by F5.
source: The earlier premotor (vs. motor) onset (Figure 3b) suggests that the movement is facilitated by F5, whereas the closer motor similarity of M1 might reflect its advanced finger control capacity due to more direct motor connections (Fogassi et al., 2001; Rathelot and Strick, 2009; Schieber and Poliakov, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from the temporal dynamics with supporting citations.

claim: The cortical grasping network transforms visual object attributes into motor plans and actions.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the cortical grasping network transforms visual object attributes into motor plans and actions.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a main conclusion from the study.

claim: Highly different coding schemes were found between the frontoparietal circuits of AIP and F5, indicating widely separated processing of visual and motor features.
source: We found highly different coding schemes between the frontoparietal circuits of AIP and F5, indicating widely separated processing of visual and motor features.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a main conclusion from the study.

claim: Visuomotor transformation is achieved effectively by visual object descriptions that activate linked motor plans in the reciprocal network of AIP and F5.
source: These findings suggest that visuomotor transformation is achieved effectively by visual object descriptions that activate linked motor plans in the reciprocal network of AIP and F5.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a main conclusion from the study.

claim: Strong feature communication between F5 and M1 suggests a common motor network that executes and refines the prepared motor plan.
source: Strong feature communication between F5 and M1 further suggest a common motor network that executes and refines the prepared motor plan.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a main conclusion from the study.

claim: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in this study (animal Z: female, 7.0 kg body weight; animal M: male, 10.5 kg).
source: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in this study (animal Z: female, 7.0 kg body weight; animal M: male, 10.5 kg).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific details about the experimental subjects.

claim: Animal housing, care, and all experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with German and European laws governing animal welfare.
source: Animal housing, care, and all experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with German and European laws governing animal welfare and were in agreement with the guidelines for the care and use of mammals in neuroscience and behavioural research (National Research Council, 2003; see also Ethics statement).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ethical compliance of the study with citation.

claim: During each recording session, monkeys grasped a total of 42–48 objects of equal weight that were placed on 8 interchangeable turntables.
source: During each recording session, monkeys grasped a total of 42–48 objects of equal weight that were placed on 8 interchangeable turntables (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design with reference to figures.

claim: In 20 recording sessions (10 per animal), each condition was repeated at least 10 times.
source: In 20 recording sessions (10 per animal), each condition was repeated at least 10 times.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific details about the experimental design.

claim: Precision and power grips applied on the handle as well as grasping and lifting the 3D-objects were detected with photoelectric barriers.
source: Precision and power grips applied on the handle as well as grasping and lifting the 3D-objects were detected with photoelectric barriers (Schaffelhofer et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the detection method with supporting citation.

claim: The monkey's eye position was monitored with an optical eye tracking system (model AA-EL-200; ISCAN Inc.).
source: Furthermore, the monkey's eye position was monitored with an optical eye tracking system (model AA-EL-200; ISCAN Inc.).
evidence: The manuscript describes the eye tracking method.

claim: All behavioural and task-relevant parameters were controlled using a custom-written control software implemented in LabVIEW Realtime.
source: All behavioural and task-relevant parameters were controlled using a custom-written control software implemented in LabVIEW Realtime (National Instruments, Austin, TX).
evidence: The manuscript describes the control software used.

claim: Monkeys were trained to grasp 49 objects in a delayed grasp-and-hold task.
source: Monkeys were trained to grasp 49 objects (Figure 1b) in a delayed grasp-and-hold task (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the task paradigm with reference to figures.

claim: The fixation epoch duration was 500–800 ms.
source: Looking at (fixating) this spot for a variable time (fixation epoch, duration: 500–800 ms) activated a spot light that illuminated the graspable object (cue epoch: 700 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing parameters for the task.

claim: The cue epoch duration was 700 ms.
source: Looking at (fixating) this spot for a variable time (fixation epoch, duration: 500–800 ms) activated a spot light that illuminated the graspable object (cue epoch: 700 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing parameters for the task.

claim: The planning epoch duration was 600–1000 ms.
source: After the light was turned off the monkeys had to withhold movement execution (planning epoch: 600–1000 ms) until the fixation LED blinked for 100 ms.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing parameters for the task.

claim: The hold epoch duration was 500 ms.
source: After this, the monkeys released the rest sensor, reached for and grasped the object (movement epoch), and briefly lifted it up (hold epoch: 500 ms).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing parameters for the task.

claim: The monkeys had to fixate the LED throughout the task with a maximum deviation of approximately 5 degrees of visual angle.
source: The monkeys had to fixate the LED throughout the task (max. deviation: ~5 deg of visual angle).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific task requirements.

claim: All correctly executed trials were rewarded with a liquid reward (juice).
source: All correctly executed trials were rewarded with a liquid reward (juice) and monkeys could initiate the next trial after a short delay.
evidence: The manuscript describes the reward contingency.

claim: Error trials were immediately aborted without reward and excluded from analysis.
source: Error trials were immediately aborted without reward and excluded from analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the handling of error trials.

claim: Seven magnetic sensor coils were placed onto the fingernails, the hand's dorsum as well as the wrist to compute the centres of 18 individual joints in 3D space.
source: Seven magnetic sensor coils (model WAVE, Northern Digital) were placed onto the fingernails, the hand's dorsum as well as the wrist to compute the centres of 18 individual joints in 3D space, including thumb, digits, wrist, elbow and shoulder.
evidence: The manuscript describes the kinematic recording method.

claim: The kinematic recording method has been described previously by Schaffelhofer and Scherberger (2012).
source: The method and its underlying computational model have been described previously (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication describing the method.

claim: Recorded joint trajectories were used to drive a 3D-musculoskeletal model adjusted to the specific anatomy of each monkey.
source: Recorded joint trajectories were then used to drive a 3D-musculoskeletal model (Schaffelhofer et al., 2015b), which was adjusted to the specific anatomy of each monkey.
evidence: The manuscript describes the kinematic analysis method with supporting citation.

claim: The musculoskeletal model was implemented in OpenSim and allowed extracting a total of 27 DOF.
source: The model was implemented in OpenSim (Delp et al., 2007) and allowed extracting a total of 27 DOF [see Schaffelhofer et al. (2015b) for detailed list of DOF].
evidence: The manuscript describes the model implementation with supporting citations.

claim: All extracted joint angles from the model were low-pass filtered, downsampled to 50 Hz and used to describe the hand configuration in a 27-dimensional joint space.
source: All extracted joint angles from the model were low-pass filtered (Kaiser window, finite impulse response filter, passband cutoff: 5–20 Hz), downsampled to 50 Hz and used to describe the hand configuration in a 27-dimensional joint space (J-space).
evidence: The manuscript describes the signal processing methods.

claim: Single and multiunit activity was recorded simultaneously using floating microelectrode arrays (FMA, Microprobe Inc., Gaithersburg, MD, USA).
source: Single and multiunit activity was recorded simultaneously using floating microelectrode arrays (FMA, Microprobe Inc., Gaithersburg, MD, USA).
evidence: The manuscript describes the recording method.

claim: In each monkey, recordings were made from a total of 192 channels of 6 individual arrays implanted into the cortical areas AIP, F5, and M1.
source: In each monkey we recorded from in total 192 channels of 6 individual arrays implanted into the cortical areas AIP, F5, and M1 (see Figure 1e–g).
evidence: The manuscript describes the recording configuration with reference to figures.

claim: In each array, the lengths of the electrodes increased towards the sulcus and ranged from 1.5 (1st row) to 7.1 mm (4th row).
source: In each array, the lengths of the electrodes increased towards the sulcus and ranged from 1.5 (1st row) to 7.1 mm (4th row).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific details about the electrode configuration.

claim: In area F5, one array was placed in the posterior bank of the inferior arcuate sulcus approximately targeting F5a and approaching the F5 convexity (F5c).
source: In area F5, one array was placed in the posterior bank of the inferior arcuate sulcus approximately targeting F5a (longer electrodes) (Theys et al., 2012a) and approaching the F5 convexity (F5c; shorter electrodes).
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrode placement with supporting citation.

claim: The second F5 array was positioned more dorsally to target F5p.
source: The second and more dorsally located array was positioned to target F5p.
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrode placement.

claim: In AIP, the arrays were implanted into the end of the posterior intraparietal sulcus at the level of area PF and more dorsally at the level of area PFG.
source: In AIP, the arrays were implanted into the end of the posterior intraparietal sulcus at the level of area PF and more dorsally at the level of area PFG.
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrode placement.

claim: In M1, both arrays were placed into the hand area of M1 into the anterior bank of the central sulcus at the level of the spur of the arcuate sulcus.
source: In M1, both arrays were placed into the hand area of M1 into the anterior bank of the central sulcus at the level of the spur of the arcuate sulcus (Rathelot and Strick, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrode placement with supporting citation.

claim: Neural activity was recorded at full bandwidth with a sampling frequency of 24 kHz and a resolution of 16 bits.
source: Neural activity was recorded at full bandwidth with a sampling frequency of 24 kHz and a resolution of 16 bits (model: RZ2 Biosignal Processor; Tucker Davis Technologies, FL, USA).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific technical details about the recording system.

claim: Neural data was synchronously stored to disk together with the behavioural and kinematic data.
source: Neural data was synchronously stored to disk together with the behavioural and kinematic data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data storage method.

claim: Raw recordings were filtered offline (bandpass cutoff: 0.3–7 kHz) before spikes were detected (threshold: 3.5x std) and extracted.
source: Raw recordings were filtered offline (bandpass cutoff: 0.3––7 kHz) before spikes were detected (threshold: 3.5x std) and extracted.
evidence: The manuscript describes the spike detection method.

claim: Spike sorting was processed in two steps: super-paramagnetic clustering followed by visual inspection using Offline sorter.
source: Spike sorting was processed in two steps: First, we applied super-paramagnetic clustering (Quiroga et al., 2004) and then revised the results by visual inspection using Offline sorter (Plexon, TX, USA) to detect and remove neuronal drift and artefacts.
evidence: The manuscript describes the spike sorting method with supporting citation.

claim: No other pre-selection was applied and single and multiunit activity have been analysed together.
source: No other pre-selection was applied and single and multiunit activity have been analysed together.
evidence: The manuscript describes the inclusion criteria for neural units.

claim: For firing rate plots, spike rates were smoothed with a Gaussian Kernel (σ = 50 ms) over time and then averaged across trials of the same condition.
source: Firing rate plots were created in order to visualize the activity of example neurons across time. For this, spike rates were smoothed with a Gaussian Kernel (σ = 50 ms) over time and then averaged across trials of the same condition (Baumann et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis method with supporting citation.

claim: The modulation depth between two conditions was defined as their absolute difference in average firing rate.
source: The MD between two conditions was defined as their absolute difference in average firing rate.
evidence: The manuscript defines the modulation depth measure.

claim: Multi-comparison tests were performed to check whether the differences in firing rate between conditions were significant (ANOVA, Tukey-Kramer criterion, p<0.01).
source: In addition, we performed multi-comparison tests to check whether the differences in firing rate between conditions were significant (ANOVA, Tukey-Kramer criterion, p<0.01; ≥10 trials/condition, ≥500 trials/session, Matlab functions: anova1, multcompare).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical testing method.

claim: A sliding ANOVA was performed in time steps of 1 ms (p<0.01; no multi-comparison correction, ≥10 trials/condition) to investigate population activity during the course of the trial.
source: To investigate the population activity during the course of the trial, we tested for significant tuning at multiple time points t using a 1-way ANOVA. Similar to the visualization of firing rates, we first smoothed all spike trains with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 50 ms) and then performed a sliding ANOVA in time steps of 1 ms (p<0.01; no multi-comparison correction, ≥10 trials/condition).
evidence: The manuscript describes the sliding ANOVA method.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to express the data variability of the J-space in a compact, lower-dimensional fashion.
source: We used principal component analysis (PCA) to express the data variability of the J-space in a compact, lower-dimensional fashion. This approach was demonstrated to be optimal for describing hand shapes (Pesyna et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes the dimensionality reduction method with supporting citation.

claim: Canonical discriminant analysis (CDA) was applied to explore the N-space (neuronal population space).
source: For exploring the N-space (neuronal population space), we applied canonical discriminant analysis (CDA).
evidence: The manuscript describes the dimensionality reduction method for neural data.

claim: CDA transforms the data in order to maximize the separation of groups (task conditions).
source: Whereas PCA creates the new coordinate system in a way that maximizes the total variance, CDA transforms the data in order to maximize the separation of groups (here: task conditions).
evidence: The manuscript explains the principle of CDA.

claim: The first axis in CDA (first canonical variable) reflects the linear combination of original variables that show the most significant F-statistic in a one-way analysis of variance.
source: The first axis in the new transform (first canonical variable) therefore reflects the linear combination of original variables that show the most significant F-statistic in a one-way analysis of variance.
evidence: The manuscript explains the interpretation of CDA components.

claim: CDA was performed based on the population's mean firing rates of a specific task epoch of interest relative to baseline activity.
source: We performed CDA based on the population's mean firing rates of a specific task epoch of interest (e.g., grasp epoch) relative to baseline activity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the input data for CDA.

claim: CDA considers only variances of the signal related to conditional differences, suppressing noise or condition-irrelevant modulations.
source: In contrast to other dimensionality reduction methods, CDA considers only variances of the signal related to conditional differences. Due to this advantage, noise or condition-irrelevant modulations get suppressed.
evidence: The manuscript explains the advantage of CDA over other methods.

claim: Procrustes analysis (PCRA) was used to test similarities or differences between multidimensional datasets of different measures and scales.
source: Procrustes analysis (PCRA) can be used to test similarities or differences between multidimensional datasets of different measures and scales.
evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose of PCRA.

claim: PCRA was used to evaluate the resemblance between the J-space and the N-space (firing rates).
source: In the context of this study, PCRA was used to evaluate the resemblance between the J- and the N-space (firing rates).
evidence: The manuscript describes the application of PCRA in this study.

claim: Both J-space and N-space representations were reduced to their highest common dimension (27 DOF) for PCRA comparison.
source: For this, we reduced both representations to their highest common dimension (i.e., 27 DOF of hand and arm) using the dimensionality reduction methods explained above (i.e., CDA for N-space).
evidence: The manuscript describes the preprocessing for PCRA.

claim: PCRA was used to translate and rotate the space of interest to minimize the sum of squared distances to the corresponding points in the reference space.
source: Then PCRA was used to translate and rotate the space of interest (e.g., N-space of M1, F5, or AIP) in a way that minimized the sum of squared distances (SSD) to the corresponding points in the reference space (e.g., J-space) (Matlab function: procrustes).
evidence: The manuscript describes the PCRA procedure.

claim: The PCRA similarity measure is a non-negative number with values near 0 implying high similarity and values approaching or exceeding 1 implying strong dissimilarity.
source: This similarity measure is a non-negative number with values near 0 implying a high similarity between the multidimensional spaces and values approaching (or exceeding) 1 implying strong dissimilarity.
evidence: The manuscript explains the interpretation of the PCRA similarity measure.

claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) was performed to illustrate and compare the many conditions in an untransformed, full-dimensional way.
source: To illustrate and compare the many conditions of our task in an untransformed, full-dimensional way, we performed hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA).
evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose of HCA.

claim: Mahalanobis distances were computed between the population activities of all possible pairs of task conditions in an epoch of interest.
source: We first computed the Mahalanobis distances between the population activities (N-space) of all possible pairs of task conditions in an epoch of interest (Matlab function: manova1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the distance measure used in HCA.

claim: An agglomerative hierarchical cluster tree was created based on the average linkage criterion.
source: This resulting distance matrix (e.g., for 50 x 50 conditions) was used to create an agglomerative hierarchical cluster tree based on the average linkage criterion (Matlab function: manovacluster), presenting the cluster solutions of an individual recording session as dendrograms (e.g. Figure 2e–f for AIP of animal Z).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering method with reference to figures.

claim: Mahalanobis distance matrices were averaged across all individual sessions to build dendrograms expressing the N-space of an animal across all recording sessions.
source: Additionally, we averaged the Mahalanobis distance matrices of all individual session to build dendrograms expressing the N-space of an animal across all recording sessions (e.g. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for AIP of animal Z).
evidence: The manuscript describes the averaging procedure for population-level analysis.

claim: For feature code correlation, spiking activity of each individual neuron was binned (bin width = 10 ms) and smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 300 ms).
source: For correlating the dynamic feature communicated within the grasping network we (1) binned the spiking activity of each individual neuron (bin width = 10 ms), (2) smoothed the firing rates with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 300 ms) and (3) aligned the firing vectors to both cue and grasp onset.
evidence: The manuscript describes the preprocessing steps for feature correlation analysis.

claim: The Euclidean distance was computed between all possible pairs of trials in the N-space within each time bin.
source: Within each of the resulting bins we then (4) computed the Euclidean distance between all possible pairs of trials in the N-space.
evidence: The manuscript describes the distance computation for feature correlation.

claim: Distance matrices from AIP, F5, and M1 were correlated for every time bin using Spearman's correlation coefficient.
source: Pairs of such matrices from AIP, F5, and M1 were then (5) correlated for every time bin (Spearman's correlation coefficient), which led to a correlation function across time for each pair of areas (AIP-F5, AIP-M1, and F5-M1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the correlation method for comparing areas.

claim: The correlation function represents for every time in the task the similarity of the encoded features between both areas.
source: This correlation function represents for every time in the task the similarity of the encoded features between both areas.
evidence: The manuscript explains the interpretation of the correlation function.
